# Job 40 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## VV. 1–2 — God's Concluding Challenge

**v. 1: “And the LORD said to Job:”** After the extended discourse of chapters 38–39 (a survey of creation's wonders), God now brings His first speech to a pointed application. The phrase marks a pause and a transition from wonder to direct moral challenge. David Guzik notes that God "answered Job's heart without specifically answering Job's questions" — the revelation of God's majesty itself was the answer.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

**v. 2: “Will the faultfinder contend with the Almighty? Let him who argues with God give an answer.”** The Hebrew term translated "faultfinder" (or "one who contends") refers to someone who would correct or reprove God. Ellicott's commentary notes the sense: "Can he that reproveth contend with the Almighty? … Art thou prepared still to dispute and contend with God?" God challenges Job: if you have been arguing with Me, now answer the questions I have just posed.

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/40.htm

Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) adds: "Does Job now still (after seeing and hearing of God's majesty and wisdom) wish to set God right?" God's questions in chapters 38–39 have exposed the vast gulf between divine and human knowledge; now He asks directly whether Job still wishes to press his case.

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/job/40.htm

Dr. Constable observes: "Yahweh ironically challenged Job to teach (or correct) Him in the matters of the universe to prove that he was equal to God and thus capable of arguing with God in court."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-40.html

**Matthew Henry** emphasises the practical application: "Communion with the Lord effectually convinces and humbles a saint… When his friends reasoned with him, he did not yield; but the voice of the Lord is powerful."

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/job/40.htm

---

## VV. 3–5 — Job's First Reply: Humbled Silence

**v. 3: “Then Job answered the LORD:”** Job's tone shifts entirely. Enduring Word notes that Job had prayed often throughout the dialogues — he was the only one of the five to speak directly to God — but now he speaks after God's revelation with a completely different spirit. "The different tone was not because Job's circumstances had substantially changed… The tone changed because while he once felt that God had forsaken him, now he felt and knew that God was with Him."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

**v. 4: “Behold, I am insignificant. How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth.”** The word rendered "insignificant" (KJV: "vile") is the Hebrew *qalalti*, meaning "of no weight" or "light." G. Campbell Morgan explains: "In the Hebrew word there is no suggestion of moral failure. Quite literally it means, of no weight. Job did not here in the presence of the majesty of God confess moral perversity, but comparative insignificance." Enduring Word quotes Spurgeon: "Surely, if any man had a right to say I am not vile, it was Job; for, according to the testimony of God himself, he was 'a perfect and an upright man.' Yet we find even this eminent saint when by his nearness to God he had received light enough to discover his own condition, exclaiming, 'Behold I am vile.'"

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

The gesture of placing the hand over the mouth is "one of the most worshipful gestures of all," writes Mason (cited by Guzik): "The act is a demonstration of total submission. One can fall on one's face and yet continue to blubber and babble. But to yield the tongue is to yield everything."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary notes: "Job's discovery a blessed one. The result of Divine teaching and of God's revealing himself to the soul. Isaiah's acknowledgment when he beheld the glory of the Lord in the temple: 'Woe is me! for I am undone.'"

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-40.html

**v. 5: “I have spoken once, but I have no answer— twice, but I have nothing to add.”** Job acknowledges he has spoken out of turn (once, even twice) and now will "proceed no further." Constable notes a key observation: "Job did not confess any sin. Therefore God proceeded to speak again. He, not Job, found it necessary to speak 'even twice.'" Job's reply here is genuine but incomplete; deeper work remains.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-40.html

Grant's Commentary adds: "Job goes deeper here than apologising for what he has said, for he expresses his judgment of himself personally. Indeed, how true it is that we ourselves, in our sinful nature, are worse than the worst thing we have ever said or done."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-40.html

---

## VV. 6–7 — God's Second Speech Begins

**v. 6: “Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind and said:”** God is still present in the storm — He has not morphed into a gentler presence. The whirlwind continues, emphasising that God's majesty has not diminished. Poole (cited by Guzik): "The whirlwind was renewed when God renewed his charge upon Job, whom he intended to humble more thoroughly than yet he had done."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

Grant's Commentary: "The whirlwind itself was intended to impress Job with the fact that every circumstance of swirling troubles and confusion was under the controlling hand of the Creator."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-40.html

**v. 7: “Now brace yourself like a man; I will question you, and you shall inform Me.”** God uses the identical phrasing from Job 38:3, signalling that He is not yet finished. Constable notes that this second discourse "began as the first one did with a challenge to Job (Job 40:6-14; cf. Job 38:1-3), but it did not end with one (cf. Job 40:1-2)." God has more to teach — now focusing on two specific creatures (Behemoth and Leviathan) rather than the broad survey of creation.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-40.html

JFB: "Since Job has not only spoken against God, but accused Him of injustice, God challenges him to try, could he govern the world, as God by His power doth, and punish the proud and wicked."

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/job/40.htm

---

## VV. 8–14 — God's Challenge: Can Job Do What Only God Can Do?

**v. 8: “Would you really annul My justice? Would you condemn Me to justify yourself?”** This verse goes to the heart of Job's error. Throughout the dialogues, Job had been more concerned with defending his own integrity than with God's justice. JFB explains: "Wilt thou not only contend with, but set aside My judgment or justice in the government of the world? condemn — declare Me unrighteous, in order that thou mayest be accounted righteous (innocent; undeservingly afflicted)."

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/job/40.htm

Ellicott: "God is about to show Job his inability to govern the world and administer judgment among men, so as to rule them morally, from his acknowledged inability to govern the more formidable animals of the brute creation."

— https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/job/40.htm

Constable: "Job had claimed God was unjust. In answering this challenge God did not argue with Job. He simply asked Job questions that made it obvious to Job that he was unable to do what he had blamed God for not doing."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-40.html

**vv. 9–11: “Do you have an arm like God's? Can you thunder with a voice like His? Then adorn yourself with majesty and splendor… Unleash the fury of your wrath; look on every proud man and bring him low.”** God challenges Job to take on the divine prerogatives — majesty, glory, the ability to humble the proud with a glance. Bradley (cited by Guzik): "'Can he,' he is asked, 'assume the royal robe of the Universal Monarch, can he array himself with honour and majesty? Can he with a glance abase the proud, and tread down the wicked?'"

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

**v. 12: “Look on every proud man and humble him; trample the wicked where they stand.”** The challenge escalates: if Job would sit in God's seat of judgment, let him do what God does — execute justice on the proud. The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: "Pride the object of God's special displeasure. The sin of fallen angels."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-40.html

**v. 13: “Bury them together in the dust; imprison them in the grave.”** The imagery is of final judgment — hiding the wicked in the dust and binding them in darkness (literally "bind their faces in hidden darkness"). This is language of death and the grave, over which only God holds ultimate power.

**v. 14: “Then I will confess to you that your own right hand can save you.”** The climactic conclusion: if Job can do all the things only God can do — exercise divine justice over the proud and the wicked — then (and only then) can he save himself. Adam Clarke's classic comment (cited by Guzik): "Salvation belongeth unto the Lord; no man can save his own soul by works of righteousness which he has done, is doing, or can possibly do, to all eternity. Without Jesus every human spirit must have perished everlastingly."

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary expands: "Self-salvation the aim of most of the religion in the world, whether Pagan, Mahometan, Jewish, or Christian. … Man's inability to save himself the ground of Christ's redemption. To exhibit that inability one of the objects of this book."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-40.html

JFB makes a striking connection to the gospel: "So as to eternal salvation by Jesus Christ (Isa 59:16; 63:5)."

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/job/40.htm

**TRADITION NOTE — Reformed (The Gospel Coalition):** The Gospel Coalition article (seen in search results) reads vv. 8–14 as God's response specifically to Job's charge about divine justice in the face of supernatural evil. "This second divine speech to Job addresses the problem of supernatural evil in the created order. … Job has questioned God's justice (40:8). So God challenges him to do the job of judging all the earth (40:11) — that is, to bring low the proud and to tread down the wicked (40:12). 'If you can do that,' says the Lord, in essence, 'then I will admit that you can save yourself. But you can't.'"

— https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/gods-sovereignty-behemoth-leviathan/

---

## VV. 15–24 — Behemoth: An Example of God's Might and Job's Weakness

**Introduction to Behemoth:** God's second speech concentrates on only two creatures — Behemoth (Job 40:15-24) and Leviathan (Job 41). Constable notes that "the second speech is not a mere afterthought about two creatures left out of the first speech. Here God accomplishes more than in the first speech, where He merely humbled Job by showing him how He is Creator and Sustainer of the natural world. Now He will convince Job He is also Lord of the moral order."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-40.html

**v. 15: “Look at Behemoth, which I made along with you. He feeds on grass like an ox.”** The name "Behemoth" is the plural of *behemah* ("beast"), likely a plural of majesty meaning "the beast par excellence." The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary provides an extensive survey: older interpreters (both Catholic and Reformed) generally identified it as the elephant; modern interpreters decisively favour the hippopotamus; some (Good, Clarke) think it an extinct creature; others view it as a poetical personification of the great Pachydermata.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-40.html

God's point: Behemoth is a creature "made along with you" — it shares creatureliness with Job, yet its power far exceeds Job's. If Job cannot contend with this fellow creature, how could he contend with its Creator?

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

**v. 16: “See the strength of his loins and the power in the muscles of his belly.”** Every part of the creature's anatomy contributes to exceptional strength. The description emphasises concentrated power in the hips and abdominal muscles, appropriate for the massive hippopotamus.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-40.html

**v. 17: “His tail sways like a cedar; the sinews of his thighs are tightly knit.”** This verse is one of the central difficulties for the hippopotamus identification, since a hippo's tail is short and stubby. Grant's Commentary argues: "Some have thought this refers to a hippopotamus, but that animal has a small tail, while behemoth 'moves his tail like a cedar' (v.17). Perhaps this animal has now become extinct, for its tail seems to resemble that of a dinosaur."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-40.html

Peake's Commentary (modern scholarship, seen in search results) calls this "an exaggeration: the tail is only a short, naked stump" — treating the language as poetic hyperbole.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-40.html

An alternative reading (noted in StudyLight.org's verse commentary): the comparison to a cedar may refer to the animal's sexual organ (the KJV "stones" is rendered "testicles" in the Douay Version), which better fits the hippopotamus.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentary/job/40-19.html

**v. 18: “His bones are tubes of bronze; his limbs are rods of iron.”** Poetic imagery for immense skeletal strength. The description fits the hippopotamus's dense, heavy bone structure suitable for an amphibious life.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

**v. 19: “He is the foremost of God's works; only his Maker can draw the sword against him.”** "Foremost" (KJV: "chief") can also be translated "the beginning of the ways of God" — possibly meaning Behemoth was among the first created (connecting to Genesis 1:24 where cattle/behemah are mentioned first). Constable notes the adult hippopotamus weighs up to 8,000 pounds, making it indeed among the largest land creatures.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-40.html

"Only his Maker can draw the sword against him" means no human can subdue this creature; only the God who created it can bring it down. Some interpret "his sword" as the hippo's own tusks or teeth — weapons given by God.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-40.html

**v. 20: “The hills yield him their produce, while all the beasts of the field play nearby.”** Behemoth is supplied with food from the mountains; it is a herbivore that poses no threat to other animals. The other beasts "play" near it without fear — it is not a predator.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

**vv. 21–22: “He lies under the lotus plants, hidden among the reeds of the marsh. The lotus plants conceal him in their shade; the willows of the brook surround him.”** This description is strongly characteristic of the amphibious hippopotamus, which submerges in rivers and marshes with only eyes and nostrils visible. The Nile setting is suggested.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-40.html

**v. 23: “Though the river rages, Behemoth is unafraid; he remains secure, though the Jordan surges to his mouth.”** The creature is untroubled by flooding. Constable notes that the definite article before "Jordan" is absent in the Hebrew, suggesting "any Jordan" — any swiftly flowing river. The hippopotamus is not native to the Jordan River, so the term is used generically for a torrent.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/job-40.html

**v. 24: “Can anyone capture him as he looks on, or pierce his nose with a snare?”** The verse is often rendered as a rhetorical question: can anyone take Behemoth by his eyes (the only part visible when submerged) or pierce his nose with a snare? The answer is no — Behemoth is untameable and uncontrollable by human means.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-40.html

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ on Job 40

### Behemoth as Dinosaur / Young-Earth Creationist View

Some conservative Protestant teachers (particularly within creation science and certain Baptist/fundamentalist circles) argue that Behemoth must be a dinosaur (specifically a sauropod like Brachiosaurus or Diplodocus), since the tail "like a cedar" does not fit the hippopotamus. This view holds that dinosaurs and humans coexisted before and/or after the Flood. Grant's Commentary (Brethren) favours this: "Perhaps this animal has now become extinct, for its tail seems to resemble that of a dinosaur. Some think the dinosaurs were destroyed in the flood, others, that some continued after the flood, and later became extinct."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-40.html

BibleHub's Q&A article notes: "Supporters of this view often highlight paleontological finds showing that certain large sauropods possessed substantial muscle mass in their torso and legs and extraordinarily thick tails… The text's stress on this tail aspect fits well with a massive dinosaur far better than with the mere short tail of an elephant or hippopotamus."

— https://biblehub.com/q/is_'behemoth'_a_real_or_mythical_creature.htm

### Behemoth as Symbol of Antichrist (Dispensational/Brethren)

Grant's Commentary uniquely sees Behemoth as symbolising Antichrist: "The character of behemoth is similar to that of many strong, capable men, men who know how to subdue others, but have no heart to be of help to them… Behemoth thus seems to be specially symbolical of Antichrist, since he is a land animal, for Antichrist will rise out of the land (of Israel), as Revelation 13:11 shows us. The first beast of that chapter rises out of the sea (of the Gentile nations), and may well be typified by leviathan."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/lmg/job-40.html

### Reformed View: Behemoth and Leviathan as Figures of Supernatural Evil

The Gospel Coalition article interprets Behemoth and Leviathan not merely as animals but as storybook embodiments of cosmic realities: "It seems Behemoth may be the storybook embodiment of the figure of death. And the Leviathan in biblical imagery is the archenemy of God." This reading connects the creatures to the Satan figure of Job 1–2, arguing that the whole second speech addresses "the problem of supernatural evil in the created order." The point is that only God can leash these forces of evil.

— https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/article/gods-sovereignty-behemoth-leviathan/

### Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word)

David Guzik emphasises the warmth of God's revelation: "God's speeches in chapters 38–39 likely came in warm, loving fellowship rather than angry harshness; it is God's goodness that leads to repentance, not His wrath alone." He stresses that Job's change came not through rebuke but through sensing God's presence, and that the Behemoth passage is primarily about the Creator–creature distinction — not about identifying the animal precisely.

— https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/job-40/

---

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship: Mythological Interpretation and Textual Questions

**Peake's Commentary** (early 20th-century critical scholarship) argues that Job 40:15–41:34 is a later addition to the poem. "The point of Job 40:8-14 is God's reply to Job's criticism of His righteousness; the description of these beasts, however, illustrates at great length man's impotence, which is only a secondary thought in the previous Divine speech. They therefore divert attention from the main issue." Peake also notes the stylistic difference: the earlier animal descriptions are "swift impressionist" sketches, while Behemoth and Leviathan are described with "heavy and laboured" accumulation of detail "proper to a natural historian."

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-40.html

Peake further reports that Gunkel and other scholars identify Leviathan with the Babylonian chaos-monster Tiamat, and Behemoth with her consort Kingu — a mythological reading rather than a zoological one.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/job-40.html

**NET Bible notes** (seen in search results) summarise: some scholars see these as real animals mythologised by pagans; others as dinosaurs (Morris); most see them as real animals (likely hippopotamus and crocodile). The NET Bible note on 38:1 (cited by Constable) captures the overall point: "In the end the point is that Job cannot have the knowledge to make the assessments he made. It is wiser to bow in submission and adoration of God than to try to judge him."

— https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Job&chapter=40&verse=15

### Catholic and Orthodox Views

The Preacher's Complete Homiletical Commentary notes that earlier Catholic interpreters (alongside Reformed ones) generally identified Behemoth as the elephant. The Douay Version renders "stones" (KJV) as "testicles" in v. 17, supporting an anatomical rather than tail-oriented reading that better suits the hippopotamus. The Vulgate, like the English versions, leaves "Behemoth" untranslated.

— https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/job-40.html

**Matthew Henry** (whose commentary is widely used across Protestant and Catholic traditions) emphasises on vv. 1–5: "Repentance changes men's opinion of themselves. Job is now convinced of his error. Those who are truly sensible of their own sinfulness and vileness, dare not justify themselves before God."

— https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/job/40.htm

---

## Summary of the Chapter's Message

The chapter falls into three movements: **(1)** God's concluding challenge to Job (vv. 1–2); **(2)** Job's humbled but incomplete response (vv. 3–5); **(3)** God's second speech, challenging Job on the moral governance of the world (vv. 6–14) and then illustrating divine power through Behemoth (vv. 15–24). Across all traditions, the central point is consistent: **if Job cannot subdue or even comprehend a fellow creature like Behemoth, how can he presume to contend with the Creator who made both of them?** The chapter prepares the way for the description of Leviathan (ch. 41) and Job's full repentance (ch. 42).
